From a cinematic standpoint, this was the most impressive season to me. I thought the acting was simultaneously the best and most lacking I’d ever seen of the entire series during this season. I thought Maya (“Robin”) gave exceptional performances as did both Jamie (“Henry”), and Noah (“Will”). I thought the “I don’t like girls” scene was well-written despite criticism from other fans. We all knew it was coming for years and I thought it was orchestrated organically and without being too preachy. I didn’t care for Kali at all. I knew she was going to return because otherwise it would have made the Duffer Brothers look “messy” as storytellers having introduced her in season 2. They couldn’t just leave her there. The legacy of the series depended on her return despite fans not wanting to see her ever again, but when she did return, I disliked her even more. I saw her as even more pointless. She felt like a liability more than an asset to the team. Her illusion of Eleven’s farewell isn’t even confirmed as being real which is the only redeeming act she would have had (hiding the kids in front of Vecna was ok, but there could have been another way.) I really disliked Jonathan and Nancy’s relationship and their scene together when the liquid concrete almost consumed them was hard to sit through, almost as hard to sit through as the Holly and Max conversation which felt like hours when Max’s home portal appeared. Most of this season felt like filler to me, if I’m being honest. There were eventful moments, sure, but I feel like those could’ve been shown in half the amount of episodes they gave us. Most of the time while watching this season, I kept thinking “is this really necessary for the plot?  The attention to these details makes it seem like it is. I’m sure it will all make sense in the end.”… And then it just didn’t. It did feel like a waste of time. I do think more main characters shouldn’t have made it til the end though, if I’m being honest, even if I didn’t want to see that happen. I think the thing that most felt like a betrayal to the fans was Hopper saying what he did to and about El. We all agreed that she deserved to finally be happy and free after this was all over. The series didn’t give her that. It gave her a tragic life, despite her friendships, filled with pain and suffering and fear… only to then make her stay behind, by choice, in the upside down while it was being eradicated? I appreciate Mike’s “happy ending for mage” speech at the end, but again, it’s not real. It’s not even possible since it would have required Kali to survive so much longer, hours after she succumbed to her wounds. And the inconsistencies with the Mind Flayer annoyed me. Is it sentient or just a large barbaric-like queen bee like in the movie Alien? I didn’t care for Nancy’s new “grandmother” look or the forced “let’s stay friends” scene at the end on the roof with her, Robin, Jonathan, and Steve either. It felt insincere and generally inauthentic to all of their characters. The finale episode just left me with so much to desire rather than feeling satisfied, but it wasn’t a complete disappointment. There were highlights that brought me joy that I will continue to take with me from this 10 year experience. All in all, I I deeply enjoyed this series and I’m grateful for the memories it has given me. I’m definitely saddened to know it’s officially over now.

STRANGER THINGS

Dear Creators, Writers, and Cast of Stranger Things,

I don’t know if this message will ever reach you, but I felt it would be wrong not to try.

I started watching Stranger Things in 2016, when I was 16 years old. I am 26 now. For almost a decade, this story didn’t just entertain me — it grew with me. I grew older, the characters grew older, and the world became heavier, darker, and more meaningful at the same time.

Stranger Things became a place where fear, friendship, loss, hope, and love could exist together. The 80s atmosphere, the silence before danger, the music, the breathing after nightmares, the way trauma stays inside a person — all of it felt deeply human. It never felt fake.

When the story reached its ending, I cried. Not because of one scene, but because a chapter of my own life quietly closed with it.

I want you to know that somewhere in the world, there is someone who truly felt your work — deeply, emotionally, and respectfully.

---

There is something else I want to share, honestly and humbly.

In real life, I am not special. I am quiet, awkward, often invisible. I fail more than I succeed. I am not powerful, not confident, not admired. Many times, I feel like a loser in a world that moves too fast for me.

But stories are where people like me survive.

In my imagination — inspired by Stranger Things — there is a character I carry with me. He is not loud. He is not heroic in the traditional sense. He is ignored in the real world, underestimated, dismissed, forgotten.

But in the Upside Down, he is something else entirely.

In that world, fear does not control him — he understands it.
He does not fight with strength — he fights with the mind.

He is quiet, deeply intelligent, observant beyond human limits. His imagination is his weapon. His thoughts bend reality. He doesn’t scream, doesn’t boast, doesn’t chase power — power gathers around him naturally.

He is so different, so unknown, that even the Mind Flayer does not understand him.

And because it cannot understand him — it fears him.

Not anger. Not hatred. Fear.

When the Mind Flayer senses him, it hesitates.
When it looks at him, it shakes.
It does not say his name — because names give power.

He is not the strongest because of violence.
He is the strongest because no one can predict him.

This character is not about ego or fantasy.
He represents what it feels like to be powerless in the real world — and what it feels like to imagine a place where intelligence, silence, and inner strength finally matter.

---

I am not writing this to demand anything, and I understand how the industry works. I simply wanted to say that Stranger Things didn’t just create characters — it created space for people like me to feel seen.

If someday, in any form, I ever had the chance to work with storytellers like you — as a creator, a thinker, a writer, or even a voice behind the scenes — it would be an honor beyond words. Not because of fame, but because you understand how to tell stories that live inside people.

Thank you for the world you created.
Thank you for the fear.
Thank you for the friendships.
Thank you for the music.
Thank you for the silence.

Stranger Things will always be a part of who I am.

With deep respect and gratitude,

A lot of the confusion about the Stranger Things finale comes from expecting a factual answer, when the ending is clearly symbolic and emotional —-> not literal.

The show intentionally does not tell us whether Eleven lived or died.

And that’s the point.

In real life, when someone leaves your life , 
a breakup, a disappearance, or death ,
you don’t actually know their inner reality.

You don’t know:
• If an ex is happy or miserable
• If they moved on or still think about you
• If someone who died is in heaven, nowhere, or somehow still present

What we do know is how we cope with not knowing.

That’s what Mike’s explanation represents.
It’s not scientific.
It’s human.

Notice the group:
• Crying
• Holding each other
• Choosing the version of the story that lets them keep living

That’s love.
That’s how people survive loss.

If the writers wanted to give a clean answer about Eleven, they would have shown it.
They didn’t … because ambiguity is the message.

Eleven stops being a lab experiment or a government target and becomes something bigger:
a memory,
a sacrifice,
a legend.

The finale isn’t asking:
“What physically happened to Eleven?”

It’s asking:
“How do we live when we don’t get to know?”

And the answer is:
We hold onto love.
We keep going.

That’s reinforced by the scene at The Squawk.

They’re not fighting monsters.
They’re doing something harder …figuring out life.

They talk about:
• Where they’re going
• What they want to do
• How they don’t want to lose each other
• How they’ll have new friends, but it won’t be the same as their bond

And Steve Harrington says:
“We should all meet up once a month.”

That line is real.

Because we’ve all said that.

Most of the time, life happens.
Work. Relationships. Distance. Responsibility.
People get busy.
Meetups fade.

But again… the show lets us choose what to believe.

We choose to believe:
• They do meet up
• They do stay connected
• Growing up doesn’t mean losing everyone

Just like when someone passes away … we choose to believe they’re still somewhere.
Just like after a breakup … we choose to believe they still think about us.

It’s not about certainty.
It’s about hope.

And the final scene completes the message.

The torch is passed.

Holly and the new generation sit down to play D&D.
Mike looks at them and smiles … not because everything turned out perfect,
but because life continues.

The story doesn’t end.
It evolves.

That’s what Stranger Things is really saying:

Growing up isn’t clean.
Goodbyes aren’t final.
And sometimes belief matters more than proof.

In early Stranger Things, the Upside Down itself was the villain before any creature showed up:
	•	toxic air
	•	sound meant death
	•	time limits mattered
	•	your body failed just by being there

The environment wasn’t a backdrop.
It was hostile by design.
Even standing still was a risk.

And every loss sent real ripples:
	•	characters hardened, not healed
	•	relationships shifted permanently
	•	the audience recalibrated what “safe” even meant

After Benny died, we knew kindness wouldn’t save you.

After Barb, we knew side characters weren’t protected.

After Bob, Alexei, Billy, Eddie—we knew bravery didn’t guarantee survival.

That’s the rule the show earned:
Good intentions don’t protect you.
Love doesn’t grant immunity.

I believe the Duffer Brothers did something remarkable by leaving the ending open to interpretation (here below the mine).

The real point is not whether Eleven is alive or dead. The ambiguity is deliberate.
What if Stranger Things is instead the story of a board game that accompanied these boys through adolescence, a shared imaginary world where Eleven exists as their invented heroine?

In this reading, the story is ultimately narrated by Mike, a boy who struggles with the idea of growing up and finds his way forward by continuing to write and tell stories. Eleven matters not as a character who lives or dies, but as a symbol: an embodiment of courage, otherness, and sacrifice, created to face fear through imagination.

The monsters and the Upside Down become metaphors, and the final image of new children playing suggests not repetition, but continuity, the passing on of imagination.

Seen this way, Stranger Things is less about parallel worlds than about the moment when childhood ends and the choice to let it fade or transform it into narrative.

Why did they even force Mike and Will together if it led nowhere? It was absolutely obvious they were building some kind of “special connection” between them, clearly more than just friendship. And then what — Will was in love with Mike for 15–20 years, and when Eleven died, meaning the main obstacle was gone, he’s just like: “Okay, guess I’ll go look for a boyfriend in LA”? What the hell? I’m not saying he had to chase Mike for another ten years, but at least try? He literally just realized this was even an option — it’s the 80s, people barely even had the concept, even if they felt it inside. Maybe wait a year or two? Maybe there’s still a chance? Screw it, the Duffer brothers had other plans. They don’t care what happened across five seasons — only what they want right now. It’s just nonsense.

Why did the Mind Flayer just leave the girl? Why did it allow the Upside Down to be destroyed? And what about the other kids? What about everything they were pumped with — all of that just got deleted together with the Upside Down, like deleting a line of text? Seriously? They literally decided to erase the story itself, forgetting that it’s supposed to be a real world with its own rules.

Where is the Mind Flayer’s projection that existed in the Upside Down — that huge silhouette?
Why did the Mind Flayer decide that some stupid spider, panicking under M4 fire, could destroy the world? That’s ridiculous. Any fighter jet would end this in 30 seconds — not to mention a nuclear strike, the strategic use of the entire nuclear arsenal. Hello? Where is the logic? He cannot destroy humanity with his body — his real power is exploiting human weakness, invading minds, spreading endlessly through hosts. That’s the only way he works. So why this direct confrontation?

Since when does destroying the Upside Down destroy the real world? They literally showed the opposite. They erased it, and the world didn’t care. That proves the worlds exist independently. The Upside Down is just a mirror — break the mirror and reality remains intact. So just close the gate and that’s it. The collision would damage that anomaly or energy source or whatever it was — the thing above the lab — but it wouldn’t destroy the real world. That’s basic logic.

Where are the Demogorgons and demodogs to protect Vecna’s main body? He was just hanging there defenseless. Yeah, Will was there, but he clearly didn’t become stronger. The writers just dropped him. Throw in three or four Demogorgons and that’s it — Will wouldn’t stop anything. He used to create them by the dozens when he only had Will, and now with ten times more power he suddenly can’t? Where’s the logic?

Why did Eleven pull Vecna out of the connection instead of finishing him off? Yes, it saved Nancy, but who told her that doing it right now was the only option? Why not finish him first? She’s facing someone clearly stronger than her, and even if Will might help, that’s not guaranteed. The writers just needed it to happen that way.

And Will himself — he says he’s going to fight, and then what? He stands somewhere random and begs Vecna to stop. Seriously? This is the same guy the whole story was building up? That’s it?

And what was the point of the coming-out? Where’s the payoff? Where’s the new strength? Nothing changes. He doesn’t become stronger. Nothing happens. All that buildup for nothing.

Why, when Vecna — with whom Will had a deep connection — gets impaled and destroyed, does Will feel nothing? The connection just disappears? He wasn’t just a victim, he was a vessel. And suddenly it’s all gone?

Why didn’t the explosion in the Upside Down wipe out everything outside it? Why didn’t the shockwave spread? Why did the gates conveniently disappear even though no one closed them?

Why was Eleven so sure no one would die? Why was she so confident the gates would destroy themselves without killing anyone? Why were the soldiers just standing there? Why not go in properly prepared and finish it? What was that ridiculous sacrifice for?

And finally — the idea that she might still be alive. We were clearly shown she was dead. Gone. Power gone. Zero. And now suddenly she’s projecting massive illusions stronger than ever? A huge storm, no interruption, nothing? Even though we know any physical contact instantly breaks the illusion. Reality touches it — it collapses. That’s established. So what are we supposed to believe now? That the rules don’t matter? That we should just “have faith”?

This is just 50%.

Gravity Falls is an American animated mystery comedy television series created by Alex Hirsch for Disney Channel and Disney XD. The series follows the adventures of Dipper Pines (Jason Ritter) and his twin sister Mabel (Kristen Schaal), who are sent to spend the summer with their great-uncle (or "Grunkle") Stan (Hirsch) in Gravity Falls, Oregon, a mysterious town rife with paranormal incidents and supernatural creatures. The kids help Stan run the "Mystery Shack", the tourist trap that he owns, while also investigating the local mysteries.

The series premiered on June 15, 2012, and ran until February 15, 2016. On November 20, 2015, Hirsch announced that the series would conclude with its second season, stating that this was "100% [his] choice" and that "the show isn't being cancelled – it's being finished" and was reaching its intended conclusion. The series ended on February 15, 2016, with a one-hour finale, "Weirdmageddon 3: Take Back the Falls".[6] Hirsch later stated that he remains open to continuing the series with additional episodes or specials, with the story continued in written form with the 2016 replica of Journal 3, the 2018 graphic novel Gravity Falls: Lost Legends and the 2024 teen-oriented novel The Book of Bill.

Gravity Falls received critical acclaim for its writing, characters, voice acting, animation, and humor. Additionally, the series won two Emmy Awards, three Annie Awards, and a BAFTA Children's Award, among various other wins and nominations. Gravity Falls garnered high viewership amongst children, teenagers, and young adults during its run and was Disney XD's highest-rated show in 2015 and early 2016, while also setting several ratings records for the network. The series has attracted a broad and passionate fandom, is considered to be an influence for many animated shows that followed it, and spawned a variety of official merchandise.

ZILA PARISHAD

A Zilla Parishad's composition includes elected members from constituencies, the chairperson/president, vice-chairperson, and ex-officio members like local MPs, MLAs, and heads of Panchayat Samitis (block councils), plus officials like the Chief Executive Officer (CEO). This apex body of the Panchayati Raj system coordinates development, approves budgets, and oversees rural governance at the district level, with members representing diverse groups like women, Scheduled Castes (SC), and Scheduled Tribes (ST).
Key Components of the Zilla Parishad:
Elected Members: Representatives directly elected by voters from different wards or divisions within the district.
Chairperson/President: The head of the Zilla Parishad, elected by the members.
Vice-Chairperson/Vice-President: Assists the Chairperson and presides in their absence.
Ex-Officio Members:
Chairpersons of all Panchayat Samitis (block-level councils) in the district.
Members of Parliament (MPs) and Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs) from the district.
Appointed Officials: The District Collector (DM) or a senior state official often serves as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) to manage administration.
Representation:
Provisions for reserved seats ensure representation for women, Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), and Other Backward Classes (OBCs).

Function:Key functions of the Zila Parishad include:
Construction and maintenance of roads, bridges, public buildings, and rural electrification.

Promoting improved farming techniques, supplying seeds, and supporting small-scale, cottage, and village industries. Implementing irrigation projects and ensuring drinking water supply.

Social Services and Education Managing primary and secondary schools, improving literacy rates, and running libraries.

Establishing and running primary health centers, hospitals, and organizing vaccination campaigns.

Implementing programs for the welfare of SC/ST, women, children, and weaker sections.

Supervising and coordinating the activities of Panchayat Samitis and village Panchayats.

Approving the budgets of Panchayat Samitis and distributing funds received from the State/Central government.

Advising the State Government on matters relating to rural development and local governance.

The Zila Parishad functions through various standing committees to ensure effective administration and development at the district level.

It acts as the district-level link between the state government and Gram Panchayats, implementing development programs and planning for the district.

BLOCK SAMITI

A Block Samiti is a link between the Gram Panchayat and the Zila Parishad. Some members of
Panchayat Samiti are elected directly by the people for a term of five years. All the Sarpanch or
Pradhan of various Gram Panchayats, members of Vidhan Sabha, Vidhan Parishad, Lok Sabha
and Rajya Sabha members who represent that block, become the ex-officio members of the Panchayat
Samiti. If people from special categories, i.e. woman, Schedule Caste, Schedule Tribe are not
represented, then they are appointed by the District Officer. There must be at least two women
members and four SC/ST members[2SC 2ST]in a Panchayat Samiti. For the smooth functioning of the
Block, the members elect a Chairman and a Vice-Chairman from amongst themselves for a period
of five years. A Block Development Officer (BDO) takes care of the administrative work of the
Block Samiti.

Key functions of the Block Samiti include:

:-Dear Stranger Things. No more new edits. No more theories. No more nights staying up late waiting for a trailer drop. Fandoms will quiet down, people will drift away, and the actors who once felt like a weird little family to all of us will eventually move on with their lives. There won’t be any countdowns, no new interviews where they laugh about behind-the-scenes moments, no more hope for ‘maybe one more season.’ Just… an ending. A line drawn in the sand. And on that final day, when the credits roll for the last time, I’ll sit there in the silence of my room, letting the emptiness settle in. Then I’ll grab my bike, roll it out into the fading evening, and ride toward the highest hill near me not to run away, but to let the moment sink in. The same way the show taught us to face the hard stuff even when it hurts.
When I reach the top, I’ll just stand there, watching the sky shift into gold and pink, letting the wind carry every memory of Stranger Things, the characters who felt like friends, the heartbreaks, the victories, the mystery, the music, the little pieces of childhood it brought back.
Because once the sun sets, it’s official: Stranger Things will slowly turn into something the world used to talk about, something kids in the future will discover instead of experience with us. It’ll become a story we try to explain to people who weren’t there for the hype, for the waiting, for the fear and the magic.
And maybe that’s what hurts the most, not just that the show is ending, but that this whole era of our lives will gently fade into a distant memory, like the glow of Christmas lights disappearing one bulb at a time.
No show will ever hit the same way. Not like this. Not like Stranger Things…

To those who hated the ending… i found someone comment this so im sharing.. This made me realize Gi-hun's final act wasn't just a rejection of the game. It was a rejection of the philosophy that created it. The Front Man believed humans are inherently selfish, driven by survival and greed, no better than horses forced to run for others’ amusement. But Gi-hun proved that wrong by doing the one thing no one else could refusing to play, even if it meant dying. His choice wasn’t strategic. It wasn’t for reward. It was to preserve something bigger than himself, something like compassion, dignity, and choice. His last words, "We are not horses. We are humans. Humans are..." The silence afterward says everything. It’s not unfinished by accident. It’s a question, a challenge, maybe even a warning. How do you define human after everything we’ve seen? The games showed us the worst. Betrayal. Cruelty. Cowardice. But they also showed us sacrifice, love, and resistance. So what are humans? Are we good? Evil? Selfish? Kind? Maybe we’re all of it at once. Gi-hun’s story doesn’t give us a clean answer. It forces you to ask what being human even means. Is humanity just compassion? If so, what about the people who created the games? They were human too. The word humanity starts to lose meaning when you realize the same species capable of kindness is also capable of horror. In the end, Gi-hun didn’t try to fix humanity. He just chose to be the kind of human he believed should exist. Not perfect. Not heroic. Just human. And maybe that’s the only answer there is.

Brilliant acting (apart from the VIPs I must say), and important messages conveyed as always, especially through that last line of Gi-hun. However, I am quite disappointed with the lack of development for this season. I don’t hate it, but I do think more could have been done with certain  things that were built up in season 2. For example, Dae-ho’s character had a lot of potential to be a character that highlights someone trying to surpass the challenges, specifically Korean, society throws at you, his struggles in the military etc, however that was discarded. I suppose that is to emphasise how humans are always lying, making up things to put themselves in a positive light, but I wish it wasn’t Dae-ho it was done to. Additionally, all the rule bending. Normally, you wouldn’t be allowed to switch teams, know what the game is, or force someone to be a player (baby), it all doesn’t seem very natural. There are many other things I could point out, but overall no I am not disappointed with this season because it’s “sad” and isn’t a super happy ending, I am disappointed because there were so many interesting ideas that were built up in season 2 left completely untouched. 6/10.

“We are not horses. We are human. Humans are..."
Gi-hun couldn’t finish that sentence—not because he didn’t know what to say, but because the truth about humanity is too heavy to put into words. Humanity is complicated. Cruel. Beautiful. Broken. It can't be explained in a single sentence. When he said, “We are not horses,” he was calling out how the VIPs treated the players as entertainment, as animals to gamble on. Just like horses used in wars and races, the players were pushed to their limits, used, discarded. That’s the entire point of Squid Game: humans being dehumanized for the sake of profit and power. And the baby who won? That wasn’t just a coincidence. Someone always has to sacrifice for someone else to live. Even if it's a child who survives, it’s because someone good gave everything. Squid Game shows that in this world, good people often suffer while bad people wait for karma to arrive if it ever does. All the players were poor. But they weren’t just chasing money they were chasing hope, a second chance, a way out. The game was built to reveal something deeper the raw truth about humanity. In the end, Gi-hun didn’t need to finish that sentence because the entire story of Squid Game already did.

I think people misunderstood the ending of Squid Game Season 3. For me, it wasn’t about whether the main character survives — it was about the message.

The story shows how people behave when pushed to their limits, especially for money. In Season 3, there’s a scene where people start arguing about killing a newborn baby just to increase their chances of winning. That reflects what actually happens in the real world — greed, selfishness, and how people stop caring about others. The baby wasn’t even a week old, but money turned everyone against her. This is exactly the kind of human nature the Front Man used to believe in.

But then Gi-hun comes in and proves something different — that even in a place full of death and greed, someone can still choose to care about others, even if they’re not related. His sacrifice at the end isn’t just emotional; it’s a complete rejection of the system. He dies so the baby can live — and that alone destroys the message the Games were trying to send.

He says, “We are not horses. We’re humans. But humans are…” and even though the line isn’t finished, the meaning is clear — humans are complex. Some are cruel, but some still have empathy. That’s why I think it’s a good ending. Not from the point of view of the main character’s survival, but from the moral side — the message that not everyone becomes a monster in hard times.

Now about the bigger picture — I think Squid Game isn’t just a Korean thing. In Season 3, when the Front Man reveals his face to Gi-hun, he says “If I die, they’ll replace me.” That means there’s a system above him. He’s not the highest authority — just a branch manager.

And in the final episode, Cate Blanchett’s character appears in Los Angeles and sees the Korean Front Man — and she recognizes him. That proves this is a global operation. It’s like a franchise, just like how banks in India have branches in every city. Squid Game has different branches in different countries, and each one has a Front Man running it. The one we saw in Korea was just one of many.

So the island in Korea was one branch. The U.S. scene at the end shows there’s another branch. And Cate’s character is likely one of the recruiters or higher-ups who know what’s going on across all branches. That’s why she didn’t need an introduction — she already knew who the Korean Front Man was.

In short, the story isn’t about “who won the Game.” It’s about what kind of person you choose to be — even when the world treats you like an animal. Gi-hun didn’t survive, but he proved that humanity can still exist inside the Game.

That’s why I liked the ending. Not because it was happy — but because it was honest.

This Horror Show Shows Who We Are
A student of mine told me about a new show called “Squid Game.” It is a South Korean “thriller series,” as they call it, which has become a pop culture phenomenon and is the no. 1 show in more than 90 countries. The show presents several hundred people who are all in great financial debt and in dire emotional states. The producers pit them against each other, even if they are very close, and make them hate each other. The winner takes millions of dollars, and the others are killed. This show wouldn’t be so horrifying if it didn’t portray our true nature. The very fact that we watch such a show enthusiastically is proof that underneath the “civilized” façade, our nature is as the show depicts.
It works like a magnet. We love to watch the struggle between good and evil, as long as we are safe from the consequences of the battle. The thing is that in this show, there is no good; there is only evil. 
Indeed, humans are the worst being in reality. What makes us so uniquely evil is the fact that we explicitly want to harm others. We do not want to eat others because we will starve unless we do so; we want to see them suffer! We derive pleasure from others’ pain, and derive the most pleasure when we are the ones inflicting it.
We often say that reality is like a jungle, where the strong eat the weak. However, in the jungle, the strong do not want to destroy the weak; they want to eat. Once they are full, they want to sleep and play, and not kill or hurt for fun. In the human jungle, we do not want to eat other people; we want to see them hurting! This is why the natural jungle thrives without any laws while the human jungle, which we mistakenly refer to as “civilization,” is disintegrating despite the laws that strive to limit our barbarity.
If we had any hopes of finding goodness in human nature, “Squid Game,” and mainly its popularity, proves that we have nothing to hope for when it comes to human nature. If we can create such shows, and if they can be so popular, then we can do such horrors in real life.
The only possible good that can come out of such a show is the realization that it is not fantasy, but an authentic depiction of who we are. Maybe if we realize this, we will be willing to do something about changing ourselves.
The current trend is to dull our awareness of the human horror show we live in by making cannabis available and legal. Indeed, the more we learn about human nature, the more we realize that perhaps it is better to numb ourselves through life until it’s over.
For now, we’re cheering at the sight of other people suffering, much like people used to cheer at the sight of poor men fighting against lions in ancient Rome. Only if we realize that it is not okay to be like that, our minds might open to other options. If such a diabolical program can be the no. 1 show in more than 90 countries, it means that the entire world is immersed in unhinged viciousness.
There is a solution, but it is demanding and must encompass the entire world if it is to succeed. To change who we are, we must initiate a worldwide educational process where such programs are forbidden and pro-human-connection programs are produced and aired. Even if they are not popular, at first, we cannot allow ourselves to be exposed to the violent poison and culture of narcissism that we consume today. They may be sweet, but they are lethal.
If people don’t want to watch shows about human connection, they can put aside their media devices and simply talk to one another. This will already be a major improvement to the current situation.
It may not sound like fun, but what is the option? To live out the “Squid Game.” Besides, after some practice, we will discover that connection and care are far more rewarding and pleasant than destruction and cruelty, and do not carry the negative side effect that is our current culture.
